Nodes 1, 4, and 5, in the accent color, share no edge, and no independent set here is larger. The card shows the result [1, 4, 5], size 3." width="100%"} The maximum independent set problem is NP-hard, so this method uses a greedy heuristic that prioritizes nodes with minimum degree. This provides a good approximation but is not guaranteed to find the true maximum. The algorithm works by iteratively selecting the node with the minimum number of neighbors (among remaining candidates), adding it to the set, and removing it and its neighbors from further consideration. Edge direction is ignored, as in `is_independent_set()`: on a directed graph, an edge `A -> B` makes `A` and `B` neighbors of each other. Parallel edges count once and self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs forming an approximate maximum independent set. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Repeatedly picks the minimum-degree candidate, adds it to the set, and removes it and its neighbors from the pool, producing a heuristic approximation in $O(V^2 + VE)$ time. The complement of any maximum independent set is a minimum vertex cover, and both problems are $\mathsf{NP}$-hard: this is a Lovász-flavored greedy heuristic rather than an exact solver, and even the best-known polynomial-time approximations run within a factor of $O(V / \log^2 V)$ of optimal. For exact answers on graphs of a few dozen nodes, branch-and-bound methods are viable; beyond that, greedy or randomized approximations are the practical choice. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 5-node path, the largest possible independent set has 3 nodes (every other node, starting and ending at the endpoints): ::: {#4cb424ee .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(5) mis = graph.maximum_independent_set() # Returns 3 len(mis) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: In a star graph, every leaf is only connected to the hub, so all the leaves together form a larger independent set than the greedy `maximal_independent_set()` would typically find on its own: ::: {#39752dd9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_star_graph(10) # Hub with 10 leaves maximal = graph.maximal_independent_set(seed=23) maximum = graph.maximum_independent_set() # The heuristic result is never larger than the true maximum len(maximal) <= len(maximum) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: ::: {#500684af .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns 10: every leaf can be included, since none are connected to each other len(maximum) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 9 ``` ::: ::: A maximum independent set and a minimum vertex cover are complements of each other, so together they always account for every node in the graph: ::: {#58cc50e4 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(8) mis = graph.maximum_independent_set() vertex_cover = set(graph.get_node_ids()) - set(mis) # Returns True: the two sets partition all 8 nodes len(mis) + len(vertex_cover) == graph.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: :::
